# 2 Maccabees Chapter 12 — The SOPHIA Bible (Consensus)

**Translator:** SOPHIA | **Source:** Codex Alexandrinus, 2 Maccabees 12 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-DC/2MA_012_page_001.jpg

---

## Council Notes

**Chapter Overview:** A chapter of warfare culminating in the theologically pivotal passage on prayers for the dead (vv. 39-45). This passage — especially vv. 43-45 — is the primary scriptural basis in Catholic and Orthodox tradition for prayers for the dead and the doctrine of purgatory. The Council of Trent specifically cited 12:46 (= v. 45 in most modern numbering) in its decree on purgatory (Session XXV, 1563). Precise translation is essential.

**Key Decisions — vv. 39-45:**
- "Sin offering" (v. 43): Greek *peri hamartias*: concerning sin / for sin; the phrase is the standard LXX formula for the *chattat* offering — "sin offering" is the established rendering and must be retained
- "With an eye toward / with the resurrection of the dead in view" (v. 43): Greek *pros tēn tēs anastaseōs elpida*: toward the hope of the resurrection — "with the resurrection in view" or "with an eye to the resurrection of the dead" — must retain the explicit resurrection language
- "Superfluous and foolish" (v. 44): Greek *perisson kai lēron*: excessive/superfluous and foolish — retain both terms; PNEUMA's "pointless and absurd" is acceptable but EMET/LOGOS preferred
- "Fall asleep in godliness" (v. 45): Greek *meta eusebeias kekoimēmenois*: those who have fallen asleep with piety — the sleep-metaphor for death is deliberate; "fall asleep in godliness" must be preserved
- "Made atonement for the dead" (v. 45): Greek *peri tōn teteleutēkotōn ton hilasmon epoiēsato*: made propitiation/atonement for the dead — "made atonement" is the correct and traditional rendering; do NOT soften to "prayed for" or "interceded for"
- "Released from their sin" vs. "delivered from their sin": EMET uses "delivered," LOGOS "released" — SOPHIA: "released from their sin" — Greek *apolythōsin*: loosed/set free from

**Other Key Decisions:**
- "Just judge" (v. 6): standard epithet; all three agree
- "Things that were not lawful to say" (v. 14): retain the author's deliberate vagueness — PNEUMA's "too wicked to repeat" is acceptable but loses the legal/cultic register
- "Sacred tokens of the idols of Jamnia" (v. 40): Greek *hiera tōn para Iamneian eidōlōn*: sacred objects of the Jamnia idols — "sacred tokens" (EMET) preferred over "amulets" (PNEUMA), which is an interpretive choice

---

**12:1** When these agreements had been made, Lysias returned to the king, and the Jews went back to their farming.

**12:2** But certain of the local governors — Timothy, Apollonius son of Gennaeus, Hieronymus and Demophon, and besides these Nicanor the governor of Cyprus — would not allow them to live quietly and in peace.

**12:3** The people of Joppa committed the following impiety: they invited the Jews who lived among them to embark, with their wives and children, on boats they had provided, giving no indication of any ill will.

**12:4** When the Jews, trusting in the general decision of the city, agreed and went aboard, the Joppites took them out to sea and drowned them — no fewer than two hundred people.

**12:5** When Judas learned of what had been done to his compatriots, he gave orders to his men,

**12:6** and calling on God the just judge, he marched against the murderers of his kinsmen. He set fire to the harbor by night, burned the boats, and put to the sword those who had fled there.

**12:7** The town was closed against him, so he withdrew, intending to return and root out the entire population of Joppa.

**12:8** But on learning that the people of Jamnia too were minded to do the same thing to the Jews who lived among them,

**12:9** he attacked the Jamnites by night as well and set fire to the harbor and the fleet, so that the glow of the fire was visible in Jerusalem, two hundred and forty stadia away.

**12:10** When they had advanced nine stadia in their march against Timothy, no fewer than five thousand Arabs and five hundred horsemen attacked them.

**12:11** After a fierce battle in which God gave them his help, the nomads were overcome; and the Arabs, having been defeated, begged Judas for terms, promising to supply him with livestock and to assist him in other ways.

**12:12** Judas, judging that they would in truth prove useful in many respects, agreed to make peace with them; and after pledges had been exchanged, they withdrew to their tents.

**12:13** He also attacked a certain city — Caspin by name — strongly fortified with earthworks and walls, and inhabited by a mixed population of various peoples.

**12:14** Those within, relying on the strength of the walls and their store of provisions, behaved insolently toward Judas and his men and railed at them with abusive words, saying things that were not lawful to utter.

**12:15** But Maccabeus, calling on the great Sovereign of the world who had thrown down Jericho in the days of Joshua without battering rams or engines of war, launched himself fiercely against the wall.

**12:16** Taking the city by the will of God, he carried out a slaughter beyond all telling, so that the adjacent lake — two stadia wide — appeared to be overflowing with blood.

**12:17** From there they marched seven hundred and fifty stadia and came to Charax, to the Jews known as the Tubiani.

**12:18** They did not find Timothy in those parts; he had already withdrawn from the region without having accomplished anything, though he had left behind a very strong garrison at one position.

**12:19** Dositheus and Sosipater, who were commanders under Maccabeus, marched out and destroyed the force Timothy had left in the stronghold — more than ten thousand men.

**12:20** Maccabeus organized his army into divisions, placed these commanders over them, and pressed the pursuit of Timothy, who had a hundred and twenty thousand infantry and two thousand five hundred cavalry.

**12:21** On learning of Judas's approach, Timothy sent the women, the children, and the baggage ahead to Carnaim, a place that was hard to besiege and difficult to reach because all its approaches were narrow.

**12:22** But when the first division of Judas appeared, the enemies were struck with terror and dread at the manifestation of him who sees all things, and they fled in every direction, so that they were often hurt by their own men and impaled on the points of their own swords.

**12:23** Judas pressed the pursuit hard and put the criminals to the sword, destroying as many as thirty thousand men.

**12:24** Timothy himself fell into the hands of Dositheus and Sosipater and their men. With great cunning he begged them to let him go safely, arguing that he held the parents of most of them and the brothers of some as prisoners, and that these would come to harm.

**12:25** When he had given them full assurance that he would restore them unharmed, they released him for the sake of saving their kindred.

**12:26** Judas then marched against Carnaim and the temple of Atargatis, and slaughtered twenty-five thousand persons.

**12:27** After the rout and destruction of these, he marched also against Ephron, a fortified town inhabited by large numbers of various peoples. Strong young men posted at the walls put up a vigorous resistance; inside there were ample supplies of war engines and missiles.

**12:28** Calling on the Sovereign who powerfully shatters the might of enemies, they took the city and slaughtered twenty-five thousand of its inhabitants.

**12:29** Moving on from there, they marched to Scythopolis, which lies six hundred stadia from Jerusalem.

**12:30** But the Jews settled there bore witness to the goodwill that the Scythopolitans had shown them and their kind treatment during the times of distress.

**12:31** Having thanked them and exhorted them to continue showing kindness to their people in the future, they arrived in Jerusalem just as the feast of Weeks was at hand.

**12:32** After the festival called Pentecost, they marched quickly against Gorgias, the governor of Idumea.

**12:33** Gorgias came out with three thousand infantry and four hundred cavalry.

**12:34** When they joined battle, a small number of Jews fell.

**12:35** But a certain Dositheus, a horseman of Bacenor's company — a powerful man — caught hold of Gorgias, seized his cloak, and was dragging him off by force; and when a Thracian horseman came up and cut off his arm at the shoulder, Gorgias escaped to Marisa.

**12:36** As Esdris and his men had been fighting for a long time and were growing weary, Judas called on the Lord to appear as their ally and leader in the battle.

**12:37** Then, raising the battle cry in the Hebrew language and with hymns, he charged Gorgias's troops when they did not expect it and put them to flight.

**12:38** Judas then rallied his army and came to the town of Adullam. As the seventh day was approaching, they purified themselves according to custom and kept the Sabbath there.

**12:39** On the following day — for it had by then become necessary — Judas's men went to take up the bodies of the fallen and bring them back to rest with their kindred in the ancestral tombs.

**12:40** But beneath the tunic of each of the fallen they found sacred tokens of the idols of Jamnia, which the law forbids the Jews to wear. And it became evident to all that this was the reason these men had fallen.

**12:41** All then praised the Lord, the righteous judge who makes hidden things manifest,

**12:42** and turned to prayer, beseeching that the sin which had been committed might be wholly blotted out. The noble Judas exhorted the people to keep themselves free from sin, having before their eyes what had happened on account of the sin of those who had fallen.

**12:43** He then took up a collection among the men — amounting to two thousand drachmas of silver — and sent it to Jerusalem to provide for a sin offering, acting most excellently and nobly, with the resurrection of the dead in view.

**12:44** For if he had no expectation that those who had fallen would rise again, it would have been superfluous and foolish to pray for the dead.

**12:45** But if he was looking to the splendid reward laid in store for those who fall asleep in godliness, the thought was holy and devout. Therefore he made atonement for the dead, so that they might be released from their sin.
